extracted.intended_audience: law students, patent practitioners (attorneys, agents), and patent examiners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the substantive requirements and defenses relevant to patentability under U.S. law, including novelty (§102), nonobviousness (§103), statutory bars, inventorship, and related evidentiary rules. Meant to instruct decisionmakers and practitioners how to evaluate whether an invention meets statutory criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty (section 102/a) — country limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge and prior use must be "in this country" to be relevant to novelty; foreign use and foreign knowledge are ignored for novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The novelty condition is not absolute — foreign uses/publications generally do not anticipate a U.S. inventor because of proof difficulties and belief that foreign knowledge is not readily accessible to those working in the U.S.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior patent publication vs unpublished patent for novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: A published patent places all that it claims and discloses into the prior art relevant to the novelty determination, whereas an unpublished patent places only the material actually claimed into the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material in a published patent counts to the extent it adequately describes the invention (i.e., enables one of ordinary skill in the field to make and understand the invention).

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of "described in a printed publication" for novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: "Described" means a description adequate to enable one with ordinary skill in the field to understand and make the invention. "Printed" broadly means material accessible to the public in tangible form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oral communications and most handwritten communications are excluded. Photographs and single indexed library copies can be publications. Distribution at a conference counts unless recipients are asked to keep it secret. The date of publication is the first date it was available to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: When an invention is considered "patented" for novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention is considered patented as of the date when the patent both is publicly available (not necessarily through publication) and confers legal rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the U.S. these events occur simultaneously on the issue date; in foreign countries they may occur on separate dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 102(e) — effective date of U.S. patent disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 102(e) pushes back to the application date the time at which the information in an issued U.S. patent becomes effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although under §102(a) a U.S. patent's information becomes effective when issued, §102(e) treats the disclosure as effective as of the earlier application filing date for prior-art purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 102(g) — first-to-invent and abandonment/suppression/concealment
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant is not entitled to a patent if, before the applicant’s invention, the invention was made in this country by another who had not abandoned, suppressed, or concealed it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abandoned, suppressed, or concealed characterize unreasonable delay by the first inventor; the first person to reduce to practice is usually the first inventor, but a later reducer can prevail if first to conceive and reasonably diligent in reducing to practice prior to the other’s conception. Priority disputes are often resolved in interference proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonobviousness (section 103) — statutory standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent may not be obtained if the differences between the subject matter sought to be patented and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious at the time the invention was made to a person having ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This codified the judicial 'invention' condition; courts require application of the Graham factual inquiries and consideration of secondary considerations to avoid hindsight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham framework — scope and content of the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the scope and content of the prior art relevant to the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior art includes the invention's own art and logically related arts (e.g., related manufacturing or material arts). Content generally includes items defined in §102 (printed publications, patents, prior US use/knowledge, earlier-filed US applications, another’s US-made invention not abandoned/suppressed/ concealed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham framework — differences between prior art and claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mislead by examining only differences and treating them as the invention; the claimed subject matter must be considered as a whole in the §103 inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham framework — level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolve the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art at the time the invention was made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors to consider include: type of problems encountered in the art; prior art solutions; rapidity of innovations; technology sophistication; educational level of the inventor; educational level of active workers in the field. The hypothetical 'person having ordinary skill' — not a layperson or genius — is the comparator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham framework — secondary considerations (objective indicia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine which, if any, secondary considerations (objective indicia) are relevant and their effect on nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondary considerations include long-felt but unsolved need, commercial success, failure of others, copying, praise, unexpected results, disbelief of experts, commercial acquiescence, and simultaneous development. The Federal Circuit requires that secondary considerations be considered (often before the final legal determination) to guard against hindsight. A nexus between the invention and the secondary considerations is required for them to be probative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of prior art for nonobviousness (enumerated sources)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art relevant to nonobviousness includes: (1) printed publications or patents worldwide published/issued before the applicant's date of invention; (2) prior use or knowledge occurring in the United States before the applicant's date of invention; (3) a U.S. patent application filed before the applicant's date that later issued; (4) another's invention made in the U.S. not abandoned/suppressed/concealed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike novelty's strict identity requirement, nonobviousness does not require strict identity — foreign patents that do not disclose all elements may still be relevant to obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material defined by §102(b) can be used in obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Material barred by §102(b) (e.g., printed publications more than one year before the U.S. application date) is also considered prior art relevant to nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A printed publication from anywhere published more than one year before the U.S. application can show obviousness even if it is not anticipatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding hindsight in obviousness determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisionmakers must avoid hindsight reconstruction — using the claimed invention as a template to piece together teachings in separate prior art pieces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the totality of evidence and take the perspective of the hypothetical person of ordinary skill at the relevant time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality / inventorship (section 102(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent will not be granted unless the named inventor is an original inventor — one who conceived the invention on his or her own; joint inventors are those who contributed to conception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Errors in named inventors can be corrected in an application or issued patent provided the error occurred without deceptive intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory bars — §102(b) general rule (one-year bar)
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor loses the right to a patent if the invention was patented or described in a printed publication in this or a foreign country or in public use or on sale in this country more than one year prior to the U.S. application date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §102(b) items include domestic/foreign patents, publications, domestic public use, and domestic on-sale events. Strict identity is not required — differences that are obvious to one skilled in the art suffice. The reference point is the application date; acts within one year before filing do not bar (the 'one-year risk-free period').

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use for §102(b) — definition and nuances
rubrics_metrics.description: Public use is a use of the product or process in its natural and intended manner; it need not be publicly visible to be public use for §102(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secret commercial use by the inventor that results in sales can be a public-use bar; conversely, secret commercial use by others unknown to the inventor usually will not bar. Experimental public uses (primary purpose experimental) may be excluded from §102(b) bar. Evidence of experimental use includes length of tests, payment received, confidentiality agreements, who conducted tests, number of tests, records, and relative duration. Subjective inventor intent carries little weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: On-sale bar specifics under §102(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: An actual commercial sale is the best evidence of an on-sale bar; sales under secrecy agreements, offers for sale, and solicitations for orders may give rise to the on-sale bar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The product offered need not be ready for delivery. Sales primarily for bona fide experimental purposes do not raise an on-sale bar. Determination requires looking at totality of circumstances and the policies behind the bar (prevent extending patent term, prevent removing inventions from public domain, favor prompt disclosure, allow reasonable time to assess economic value).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof re: public use and experimental use
rubrics_metrics.description: The challenger must first make a prima facie showing that the invention was publicly used; the patent owner then must come forward with convincing evidence to counter that showing (e.g., evidence of experimental use).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit has held that the burden of proof never shifts to the patent owner, but the patent owner will need to introduce evidence if the challenger establishes a prima facie case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 102(c) — abandonment
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor loses the right to obtain a patent if he or she abandons the invention; abandonment requires intent to abandon and is distinct from §102(g) abandonment/suppression/concealment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 102(c) decisions are rare. Intent to abandon can be express or implied by long and unexcused delay in filing. Abandoning a patent application does not, by itself, constitute §102(c) abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations — relevance and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of secondary considerations does not automatically prove nonobviousness; they merit attention only when they serve as objective indicia and when a nexus between the invention and the secondary considerations is shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial success, long-felt need, failed efforts of others, copying, praise, unexpected results, disbelief of experts, commercial acquiescence, and simultaneous development can be probative, but success may be due to non-inventive reasons (market position, advertising) and thus irrelevant absent a nexus.
